Branched How many years did it take them to develop Infamous? And how many developers were there? 
Jun 3, 2026, 1:23:23 PM CDT

The development of the original inFamous (2009) was quite a feat for Sucker Punch Productions, especially considering they were transitioning from the more stylized, level-based Sly Cooper series to a gritty, open-world superhero game.

Development Timeline & Team Size

  • Time to Develop: It took approximately 3 years to complete the game.
  • Team Size: The project was built by a relatively small team of about 60 people.

A Few Fun Facts from the Dev Cycle

  • The "True" Transition: inFamous was Sucker Punch’s first foray into open-world design. For a team of 60, creating a fully interactive "Empire City" with a morality system was a massive technical hurdle.
  • Growth over time: By the time they developed the sequel, inFamous Second Son for the PS4, the team had nearly doubled to about 110 people—which is still considered "lean" for a major AAA studio like Naughty Dog or Santa Monica Studio.
  • The Original Pitch: Early in development, the game was much more "superhero-lite" and even featured a building mechanic that was eventually scrapped in favor of the parkour and electrical combat we see in the final game.

It’s pretty impressive they pulled off that level of polish with only 60 devs—definitely speaks to how efficient they had to be with their systems.

Branched  so it sounds like they reused the engine from Sly Cooper to build this. 
Jun 3, 2026, 1:23:24 PM CDT

That is a very logical assumption—especially since they went straight from Sly 3 into inFamous—but the reality was actually much more brutal for the team.

They could not just reuse the Sly Cooper engine. The engine they used for the PS2 games (internal code name SPACKLE) had to be almost entirely rewritten from scratch to work on the PlayStation 3.

In a postmortem breakdown of the game's development, the team admitted they drastically underestimated the "cost of realism" and the technical leap to the PS3. It turned into a massive hurdle for two major reasons:

1. The PlayStation 3's "Cell" Architecture

The PS3 was notoriously difficult to program for. Its Cell processor relied on one main core and seven specialized co-processors (called SPUs). The old Sly Cooper code, which was designed for the single-core architecture of the PS2, simply didn't understand how to split tasks across all those different processors. Sucker Punch had to completely rework their underlying physics and rendering pipelines just to get the code to run on the new hardware.

2. The 10-Month Art Engine Blindspot

Because they hadn't started rewriting the engine until Sly 3 completely wrapped, Sucker Punch didn't actually have a working graphics pipeline or engine running on the PS3 for the first 10 months of inFamous’s development.

This meant the art team was essentially flying blind. They were trying to learn how to transition from stylized, cel-shaded, low-polygon cartoon assets to high-detail, realistic city textures and dynamic lighting without an actual game engine to test their assets in.

What Did Carry Over?

While the engine code itself was mostly a fresh start, their design logic definitely carried over:

  • The Physics Foundation: Sucker Punch has always been obsessed with physics (dating all the way back to their N64 game, Rocket: Robot on Wheels). The way Cole moves, grabs ledges, and reacts to gravity built directly on the platforming telemetry they perfected in Sly.
  • The "Hub" Mentality: The open, multi-stage heist hubs from Sly 2 and Sly 3 served as the mental blueprint for how they laid out the three islands of Empire City.

So while they technically evolved their proprietary studio tools, they spent a massive chunk of those three years building a brand-new technical foundation just to handle the PS3's raw power.

Branched  for inFamous running on my Mac silicone, are there any mods or upgrades I can do past this point? 
Jun 3, 2026, 1:23:24 PM CDT

Running the original inFamous on Apple Silicon via RPCS3 (the PS3 emulator) is a massive stress test for your Mac. Because inFamous pushes the PS3's unique Cell architecture to its absolute limits, emulating it requires immense CPU processing power.

While traditional game mods (like custom skins or textures) are virtually non-existent for this title, you can apply several emulator-level upgrades, config tweaks, and patches to significantly stabilize and enhance your performance.

1. Enable Canary & Game Patches (The FPS Unlock)

RPCS3 has a built-in patch manager that lets you modify game behavior at runtime. This is the closest thing to a "mod" you can get, and it is mandatory for a smooth experience.

  • How to open: Right-click inFamous in your RPCS3 game list and select Manage Game Patches. Click Download Latest Patches if you haven't recently.
  • Essential Patches to Check:
    • Unlock Framerate: By default, the game is hard-locked to 30 FPS. Unlocking it allows your Apple Silicon cores to push past that barrier when overhead is available.
    • Disable Motion Blur / Disable Depth of Field: Turning these off visually cleans up the image and saves precious processing cycles on your GPU.

2. Crucial RPCS3 Configuration Upgrades

Because Apple Silicon handles multi-threading differently than Intel/AMD x86 chips, standard RPCS3 settings will cause immense lag. You should right-click the game, choose Create Custom Configuration, and apply these specific tweaks:

TabSettingAdjustmentWhy It Matters
CPUSPU Block SizeSet to MegaCrucial for performance in heavy open-world games like inFamous.
CPUPreferred SPU ThreadsSet to 3 or 4Prevents RPCS3 from flooding your Mac's Efficiency cores (E-cores) and forces it to utilize the high-performance cores (P-cores).
GPUResolution ScaleStick to 100% (720p) or 150% (1080p) MaxDo not try to push 4K. Apple Silicon uses MoltenVK to translate the game's Vulkan instructions into Apple's native Metal API. Pushing the resolution too high introduces massive translation overhead.
AdvancedVBlank FrequencyMatch your monitor (e.g., 60Hz or 120Hz)Works hand-in-hand with the unlocked frame rate patch to smooth out frame pacing.

⚠️ Expect a Shader Compilation "Stutter" Zone: The first time you execute a new power, enter a new district, or cause an explosion, the game will hitch for a split second. This isn't a problem with your hardware; it's just RPCS3 compiling the PS3's shaders into Apple Metal code on the fly. Once a shader is compiled, it's saved to your disk, and that specific stutter won't happen again.

If you are running a Pro or Max tier chip, these tweaks can often stabilize the game into a playable 30–45 FPS range. If you are on a base M-series chip, keeping the resolution strictly at native 720p is your best bet to avoid massive frame drops during heavy electrical combat.

On Apple Silicon (your M2 Mac Mini and MacBook Air), ASMJIT is greyed out because it is an x86-only recompiler. It was designed specifically for Intel and AMD processors to translate PS3 code.

For your Mac's ARM-based architecture, RPCS3 uses the LLVM recompiler instead. This is actually a good thing—LLVM is generally more efficient and is the "gold standard" for performance on macOS.

Since you're troubleshooting the black screen and performance, here is how to handle the CPU Tab settings for your specific hardware:

1. Correct CPU Settings for M2/Apple Silicon

  • PPU Decoder: Set to Recompiler (LLVM).
  • SPU Decoder: Set to Recompiler (LLVM).
    • Note: This replaces the ASMJIT option you were looking for.
  • Enable SPU Cache: Keep this Checked. This is vital for inFamous so the emulator doesn't have to re-translate the lightning effects every single time they appear.

2. The "Thread" Sweet Spot

Since you found that forcing threads to 3 caused a crash, your M2 chip will handle it much better if you use Priority rather than Quantity:

  • Preferred SPU Threads: Set to Auto.
  • SPU Priority: Set to Major or Above Normal.
    • Why: This tells macOS to give the PS3's SPU tasks the highest priority on your Performance cores without "locking" the number of threads, which avoids the bottleneck that likely caused your black screen.

Quick Fix for the Black Screen (Specific to macOS)

If you have LLVM selected and it still black screens:

  1. Go to the GPU Tab.
  2. Ensure Graphics Device is set to Vulkan.
  3. Ensure Framelimit is set to Auto or 60.
  4. Lower the Resolution: If you were trying to scale to 150% or 200%, drop it back to 100% (1280x720) just to get past the boot sequence. You can always bump it back up once you're successfully in the game.

Since you're running this on your M2 Mini, the CPU is definitely powerful enough to handle inFamous; the "black screen" is almost certainly just a handshake issue between the Write Color Buffers setting (which must be ON) and the LLVM compiler finishing its job.

How far into the boot process are you getting now? Is the "FPS" counter at the top of the window moving, or is it stuck at 0?

Branched It was either the spu threads at 3 or the spu block size set to mega that caused the black screen
Jun 3, 2026, 1:23:25 PM CDT

Ah, that makes total sense. Changing those two specific settings can easily cause a total thread lock on Apple Silicon, preventing the emulator from initializing the game's audio and video pipelines altogether.

Here is exactly why that happened, and how you can safely adjust them to keep the performance benefits without crashing the game:

Why "Mega" and "3 Threads" Broke It

  1. The SPU Block Size Issue: Setting the block size to Mega forces the emulator to bundle massive chunks of SPUs (the PS3 co-processors) together for execution. While x86 chips (Intel/AMD) can sometimes brute-force this, Apple Silicon's execution pipelines can get overwhelmed by blocks that large, causing the graphic thread to time out before the game can even render the first frame.
  2. The SPU Thread Limit Issue: Hard-coding preferred SPU threads to 3 or 4 can sometimes starve the rest of the emulator's backend. RPCS3 needs free CPU threads to handle things like PPU (the main PS3 processor), OS calls, and memory management. If your Mac's performance cores get entirely locked up by those 3 forced SPU threads during bootup, the whole system freezes.

The Stable "Middle Ground" Settings

To get the game running again without completely losing the performance tuning we aimed for, change those two settings back to these safer, Apple-Silicon-friendly baselines:

  • SPU Block Size: Set this to Safe (or Standard). This is the absolute highest priority for stability. It uses smaller data chunks that play much nicer with Apple's unified memory architecture.
  • Preferred SPU Threads: Set this to Auto. Instead of forcing a specific number, let RPCS3 dynamically assign threads.

One More Tweak for Performance

Since we are resetting threads to Auto, go to the CPU tab and make sure SPU Cache is set to Executable Subroutines (ASMJIT) if it isn't already. This allows your Mac to compile and cache the game's SPU code much more efficiently, giving you a frame rate bump without risking the black screen.

Change those back, give the game a fresh boot, and you should see the Sucker Punch logo pop up!

Branched So I am back to the game black screening
Jun 3, 2026, 1:23:25 PM CDT

That is incredibly frustrating, especially after messing with the configuration. Black screens in RPCS3—particularly on Apple Silicon and with games like inFamous—usually mean the emulator is hanging while trying to initialize the graphics pipeline or compile the initial shaders.

Since inFamous pushes the PS3's Cell architecture so hard, it is highly sensitive to specific settings. Let's get you past the black screen. Try these troubleshooting steps in order:

1. Disable "Unlock Framerate" Temporarily

If you just turned on the Unlock Framerate game patch, turn it off and try booting.

  • Why: Some versions of the inFamous game patches require specific game update versions (like v1.01 or v1.02). If your game boot files don't perfectly match the patch requirements, the game will crash to a black screen before the main menu can even render.

2. Check the "Write Color Buffers" Setting

This is the number one cause of black screens in Sucker Punch games on RPCS3.

  1. Right-click inFamous and select Change Custom Configuration.
  2. Go to the GPU tab.
  3. Check the box for Write Color Buffers.
  • Why: inFamous uses complex post-processing effects for its lighting and electricity. Without this setting enabled, the emulator fails to pass the rendered image to your screen, leaving you stuck in pitch blackness while the game technically runs silently in the background.

3. Clear the Pipeline Cache

Sometimes a corrupted shader or pipeline cache from a previous crash will prevent the game from booting entirely.

  1. Right-click inFamous in your game list.
  2. Hover over Remove at the bottom of the context menu.
  3. Select Clear Pipeline Cache (do not clear your game data or save data!).
  4. Re-boot the game. It will take a minute to recompile the basic startup shaders, but it often clears the block.

4. SPU Loop Detection

Go back to your CPU tab in the custom configuration and ensure SPU Loop Detection is checked (enabled). This setting allows the emulator to catch infinite loops in the game code—something inFamous is notorious for doing during its loading sequences—and force the CPU thread to keep moving forward.

If it still refuses to boot, take a quick peek at the Log window at the bottom of your RPCS3 interface right after the black screen happens. What color are the last few lines of text (Red or Yellow), and what does the error say?

Branched So it sounds like this architecture was good at crunching flooding point numbers. Was there anything else it was good at?
Jun 3, 2026, 1:23:26 PM CDT

Yes, absolutely. Because floating-point math is the foundation for 3D physics, vectors, and geometry transformations, that is what the Cell is most famous for. But the SPUs were essentially high-speed stream-processing engines, which made them incredibly dominant at a few other specific, math-adjacent workloads:

1. High-Definition Video Decoding and Encoding

The Cell was originally envisioned as a premier multimedia processor for the HD era, and it was an absolute beast at video processing.

  • The Blu-ray Heavy Lifter: When the PS3 launched in 2006, playing back a 1080p Blu-ray disc required an immense amount of processing power to decode video codecs like H.264 in real time. Most desktop computers at the time would choke and stutter trying to play raw 1080p video.
  • How the Cell Handled It: Because video streams can be easily chopped up into predictable, sequential blocks of data, the Cell could feed one frame to SPU 1, the next to SPU 2, and so on. The PS3 decoded high-bitrate HD video effortlessly without dropping a single frame, making it the most reliable Blu-ray player on the market for years.

2. Audio Processing and Software Synthesis

In traditional game engines, audio mixing is often a compressed, low-priority afterthought because the main CPU is too busy handling game logic. The PS3 flipped this.

  • Game developers could dedicate an entire SPU strictly to audio.
  • This allowed for real-time dynamic acoustic modeling. In games like Killzone or Uncharted, the engine could calculate how sound waves would physically bounce off a concrete wall versus a wooden crate, adjusting the reverb, echo, and occlusion on the fly.
  • It was also used for massive multi-channel audio mixing (like uncompressed 7.1 LPCM surround sound) completely in software without needing a dedicated hardware audio chip.

3. Cryptography and Hashing

The SPUs were exceptionally fast at processing cryptographic algorithms (like AES encryption or SHA-1 hashing).

  • The Security Protocol: Sony relied heavily on this for the PS3’s digital rights management (DRM) and system security. The isolated nature of the SPU’s "Local Store" memory meant that encryption keys could be processed in a secure bubble, entirely hidden from the rest of the system RAM.
  • The Distributed Computing Power: This cryptographic speed is exactly why the PS3 was a premier hardware choice for Folding@home—a distributed computing project run by Stanford University. Millions of PS3 owners left their consoles running overnight to crunch complex molecular biology equations and simulate protein folding to help research cures for diseases.

4. Fast Fourier Transforms (FFT) & Signal Processing

In medical imaging, telecommunications, and radar systems, processors constantly need to perform a mathematical operation called a Fast Fourier Transform (which converts a signal from its time domain to a frequency domain). Because the Cell was so fast at handling matrix operations and signal processing, IBM actually sold specialized blade servers packed with Cell processors to hospitals for real-time 3D medical imaging (MRI and CT scans) and to seismic research companies for oil and petroleum exploration.

What was it terrible at?

To contrast all of this, the Cell was downright awful at Integer Math and Branch Prediction.

If a piece of code had a ton of complex "If/Else" logical conditional statements—like standard game logic, managing a user interface, or parsing a database—the SPUs couldn't handle it efficiently. They lacked the advanced branch-prediction hardware that traditional Intel or AMD chips used to guess which direction a piece of code would go. If the SPU guessed wrong, its entire pipeline stalled out completely.

This is why game development on the PS3 was such a balancing act: developers had to keep the messy, logic-heavy code on the weak main core (the PPE) while scrubbing all the data clean, turning it into pure, predictable streaming math, and hurling it over to the SPUs.

Branched Is there anything that is like the PS3? Why did they choose to do that?
Jun 3, 2026, 1:23:26 PM CDT

Nothing quite like the PS3's Cell architecture exists in the consumer computing space today. It was a fascinating, radical, and ultimately dead-end branch of computer history.

To understand why they built it—and what came closest to it—we have to look at the massive gamble Sony, IBM, and Toshiba took in the early 2000s.

Why Did They Choose to Do This?

When Sony began planning the PS3 in 2001, they started with a totally clean slate. Looking five to ten years into the future, the engineers identified a massive upcoming hurdle in computer engineering known as the memory wall.

Traditional, powerful CPUs were getting so fast that they spent up to 80% of their time sitting idle, waiting for data to travel from the main system RAM into the processor's cache. No matter how fast you made the clock speed ($GHz$), memory latency was choking performance.

Sony’s solution was the Cell Broadband Engine, designed with a completely different philosophy:

  • Bypassing the Memory Wall: Instead of using huge, complex circuitry to guess what data a CPU might need next (like Intel or AMD did), the Cell forced the developer to manually stream tiny chunks of data directly into the isolated, hyper-fast "Local Store" memory of the SPUs. By shifting memory management from hardware to software, data crunching and data transferring could happen entirely in parallel.
  • The "One Chip to Rule Them All" Vision: Sony and Toshiba didn’t just want a gaming chip. They envisioned the Cell as a universal processor. The plan was to manufacture this one architecture at a massive scale and put it inside everything—HDTVs, medical imaging devices, home servers, and cell phones. Sony even originally planned to put two Cell chips inside the PS3, bypassing a traditional graphics card entirely and letting the SPUs handle both logic and graphics.

While they had to rush to add a standard Nvidia graphics card right before the 2006 launch when that dual-chip plan proved too difficult, the single-Cell design remained a masterclass in raw mathematical throughput.

Is There Anything Else Like the PS3?

Because the Cell was so difficult to program for, consumer electronics completely abandoned this "asymmetric hybrid" design. However, the concept of the PS3 lives on in a few very specific places:

1. Modern GPGPU (General-Purpose Graphics Processing Units)

The true spiritual successor to the PS3 isn't a modern CPU; it's a modern graphics card utilizing Compute Shaders. Technology like Nvidia’s CUDA or modern AI accelerators share the exact same DNA as the PS3's SPUs. They rely on taking incredibly predictable, massive parallel workloads (like physics, matrices, and vector math), breaking them into thousands of tiny pieces, and executing them simultaneously without traditional CPU caching. Sony essentially built a modern GPU computing framework, they just mistakenly put it inside the central processor socket.

2. The US Air Force "Condor Cluster" Supercomputer

Because the Cell processor was so absurdly fast at raw floating-point math, the PS3 found an accidental second life in scientific and military supercomputing. In 2010, the US Air Force built a supercomputer nicknamed the Condor Cluster by networking 1,760 PlayStation 3 consoles together.

Because Sony was selling the PS3 hardware at a financial loss to get it into living rooms, the Air Force realized it was the cheapest way in human history to acquire massive parallel computing power. The cluster was used to process high-definition satellite imagery and cost roughly 10% of what a conventional supercomputer would have cost at the time.

The Structural Legacy: Today's mobile processors (like Apple Silicon or Qualcomm chips) use something called a Heterogeneous Architecture—combining fast "Performance" cores with efficient "Efficiency" cores. While that sounds like the PS3's layout, it's completely symmetric in how it handles memory and instructions. The PS3's brutal model of a general-purpose manager core commanding completely naked, cacheless math sub-processors remains a unique artifact of a time when the rules of modern computing hadn't been set yet.

To see a great breakdown of how this incredibly complex processor actually impacted game development over the console's lifespan, you can watch this technical retrospective on the PS3's unique architecture, which explains how studios like Naughty Dog eventually mastered the hardware to push graphics an entire generation ahead.

Branched How does this differ from the PS4?
Jun 3, 2026, 1:23:26 PM CDT

The transition from the PS3 to the PS4 in 2013 was essentially an architectural U-turn. Sony realized that while the PS3’s exotic, hyper-parallelized Cell processor was incredibly powerful in theory, it was burning out developers and crippling launch lineups.

For the PS4, Sony completely abandoned the Cell processor and moved to an architecture that looks exactly like a standard, modern PC.

1. Radical Shift in CPU Design (Goodbye SPUs)

Instead of a single weak manager core paired with seven GPU-like "dumb" workers, the PS4 uses an AMD "Jaguar" APU (Accelerated Processing Unit).

  • Traditional, Symmetric Cores: The PS4 features 8 identical, symmetric CPU cores. They use standard x86-64 architecture—the exact same instruction set used by Intel and AMD desktop computer chips.
  • Out-of-Order Execution: Unlike the PS3's SPUs, which had to be fed data manually step-by-step, the PS4’s cores can look ahead at code, predict what needs to happen, and execute tasks out of order to keep things moving efficiently.

For developers, this was a massive relief. Writing code for the PS4 felt like writing code for a standard PC, allowing them to use standard multi-threading techniques without micromanaging memory.

2. True Unified Memory (GDDR5)

As you found during your emulator troubleshooting, managing memory on the PS3 is a nightmare because it's split up into tiny, isolated pools (like the SPU's 256KB Local Store) and separated into 256MB of system RAM and 256MB of video RAM.

The PS4 fixed this by introducing 8 gigabytes of Unified GDDR5 RAM.

  • There are no separate pools for the graphics card and the processor.
  • Both the CPU and the GPU look at the exact same chunk of ultra-fast memory. If the CPU loads a texture or a physics mesh into RAM, the GPU can see it instantly without needing to copy it across a slow system bus.

3. Moving Parallel Math to the GPU (GPGPU)

So, what happened to all that crazy vector math the SPUs used to do? In the PS4 era, that work was handed off to where it actually belonged: Compute Shaders on the GPU.

The PS4’s graphics chip was specifically modified to support GPGPU (General-Purpose computing on Graphics Processing Units). Instead of forcing developers to write custom microcode for weird CPU co-processors to handle things like fluid physics, collision detection, or dynamic lighting, they could just use the massive parallel processing power of the AMD Radeon GPU via standard computing shaders.

Sucker Punch's Relief: inFamous Second Son

To see how much this changed things, you only have to look back at Sucker Punch.

When they built inFamous Second Son for the PS4 launch, they didn't have to spend 10 months building a graphics pipeline blind. Because the hardware used standard PC architecture, they could build their engine on a PC, test it immediately, and port it seamlessly to the console. They were able to achieve astonishing particle effects (like Delsin’s smoke and neon powers) using standard GPU compute shaders rather than fighting a hyper-complex cell matrix.

Essentially, the PS3 was a highly experimental, decentralized jigsaw puzzle. The PS4 streamlined everything into a cohesive, developer-friendly powerhouse.

Branched So for a ps3 they had 8 decentralized CPUs, were these more cpu or more like gpus?
Jun 3, 2026, 1:23:26 PM CDT

You have hit on one of the most famous architectural debates in computer science history. The short answer is: The SPUs were structurally much closer to a modern GPU than a traditional CPU.

In fact, when IBM, Sony, and Toshiba were designing the Cell processor in the early 2000s, Sony originally intended for the Cell to handle both the central processing and the graphics processing for the PS3, entirely eliminating the need for a traditional graphics card.

While they eventually abandoned that idea and rushed to add a standard Nvidia GPU (the RSX "Reality Synthesizer") right before launch, the SPUs retained that heavy, GPU-like DNA.

Here is exactly how those SPUs bridged the gap between CPU and GPU design:

1. Vector Math Specialists (SIMD)

Traditional CPUs of that era were built for scalar processing—handling one piece of data at a time, but doing it very flexibly (e.g., "If X is true, jump to step B").

GPUs are built for vector processing (SIMD: Single Instruction, Multiple Data). They take a single command and apply it to a massive array of numbers simultaneously—like changing the brightness on a million pixels at once. The PS3's SPUs were pure SIMD engines. They were designed specifically to crunch massive streams of floating-point math, which is exactly how 3D graphics, vertices, and complex physics vectors are calculated.

2. No Memory Cache (Scratchpad Memory)

A normal CPU spends a massive amount of physical space on "Cache" (L1, L2, L3 cache). The CPU guesses what data you might need next, pulls it from your RAM, and keeps it close by so it doesn't waste time waiting.

The SPUs had zero cache. Instead, each SPU had a tiny, 256-kilobyte bubble of dedicated memory called Local Store. The developer had to manually tell the SPU exactly what data to grab from the main RAM, let the SPU crunch it, and then manually pull it back out via DMA (Direct Memory Access) transfers. This manual pipeline is highly characteristic of how modern software feeds data to a GPU.

How Sucker Punch Weaponized This for inFamous

When Sucker Punch was struggling to make inFamous run smoothly, they realized the Nvidia GPU inside the PS3 couldn't handle all the dynamic lighting, particle effects, and screen-space ambient occlusion (SSAO) required for Cole's electrical powers.

So, they treated the SPUs like a second graphics card.

They offloaded tasks that normally belong to a GPU—like culling invisible geometry, calculating vertex deformations, and rendering post-processing effects—and forced the SPUs to do them. By using the SPUs as a hybrid CPU/GPU worker colony, they freed up the actual Nvidia graphics card to focus entirely on basic texture mapping and outputting the final image.

This is exactly why your emulator has to work so hard: it isn't just emulating a central processor; it is essentially emulating an entire secondary, highly specialized graphics processing array.

Branched  so the PS3 system seems to be very parallelized. In comparison to a computer of that time, the PS3 has many cores, as opposed to one strong core. 
Jun 3, 2026, 1:23:26 PM CDT

You hit the nail on the head. That is exactly why the PS3 was both a technical marvel and a total nightmare for developers.

In 2006, when the PS3 launched, the mainstream PC and console world was just barely dipping its toes into dual-core processors. Most consumer PCs still relied on one single, highly powerful core that did everything sequentially.

The PS3 threw that entire philosophy out the window. Sony, Toshiba, and IBM designed the Cell Broadband Engine, which was fundamentally an early, radical experiment in massive parallel processing.

The Architecture: One Boss, Seven Workers

Instead of having multiple identical cores (like a modern quad-core CPU), the Cell engine used an asymmetrical layout:

  • The PPE (Power Processing Element): This was the "main" core. By the standards of 2006, it was actually quite weak. It wasn't designed to brute-force heavy lifting; its primary job was to act as the manager, handling the game's basic OS tasks and directing traffic.
  • The SPUs (Synergistic Processing Elements): There were 7 active co-processors (technically 8, but 1 was permanently disabled to increase manufacturing yields, and 1 was reserved strictly for the PS3's operating system, leaving 6 for game developers).

These SPUs were incredibly fast at math, but they were "dumb." They had no cache memory of their own; developers had to manually feed them tiny chunks of data, wait for them to crunch the numbers, and pull the data back.

The Parallel Dilemma

To see how radical this was compared to a 2006 PC, look at how a game's engine had to change:

System ComponentTraditional 2006 PC ApproachThe PS3 "Cell" Approach
Game LoopLine up Physics, AI, Graphics, and Audio in a single, straight line. The CPU finishes one task, then moves to the next.Break the game down into hundreds of tiny, independent jobs.
ExecutionRely on clock speed ($GHz$) to get through the line as fast as possible.Send enemy AI to SPU 1, electrical physics to SPU 2, audio mixing to SPU 3, and collision detection to SPU 4—all at the exact same millisecond.

Why This Explains Your Emulation Struggles

This brings us right back to why inFamous is giving your modern M2 Mac such a workout.

When you run an emulator like RPCS3, your Mac can't just run the game code naturally. It has to use its own CPU cores to pretend to be that incredibly specific, highly parallelized hardware. Your Mac has to constantly simulate the weak manager core (PPE) talking to six hyper-fast worker cores (SPUs), keeping all of their memory transfers perfectly synced up in real time.

If one SPU thread gets even slightly out of sync on your Mac, the whole delicate house of cards collapses, resulting in the exact thread locks and black screens you've been troubleshooting!

Branched I guess one of my questions is how can the sbu be specialized for floating Point logic and not integer logic? Is it because floating Point relies heavily on base 2 operations?
Jun 3, 2026, 1:23:27 PM CDT

That is a really intuitive line of thinking, but the division between floating-point and integer performance actually comes down to a different fundamental engineering choice: how much physical space (silicon) you allocate to complex mathematical circuits, and how those circuits are laid out.

Both integers (whole numbers) and floating-point numbers (decimals) are processed in base-2 binary by a computer. The reason the PS3’s SPUs (Synergistic Processing Elements) were absolute monsters at floating-point logic but mediocre at integer logic is due to two main architectural decisions:

1. The Design of the ALU vs. the FPU

Inside a processor, different types of math require completely different physical circuits:

  • ALU (Arithmetic Logic Unit): Handles basic integer math (like 2 + 2) and logical operations (AND, OR, NOT). These circuits are relatively simple and small.
  • FPU (Floating-Point Unit): Handles scientific notation decimal math (like $3.14159 \times 1.414$). Because a floating-point number has to store a sign bit, a significand (the base digits), and an exponent, multiplying them requires massive, complex barrel shifters, adders, and alignment circuits.

When IBM and Sony designed the SPUs, they looked at their "real estate" budget and made a deliberate trade-off. They packed each SPU with a massive, hyper-optimized, wide pipeline dedicated purely to floating-point math.

To save space and power, they didn't give the integer units that same level of hardware luxury. The integer pipelines in the SPU were narrower and lacked the advanced hardware features (like deep out-of-order execution or hardware division) found in traditional desktop CPUs.

2. The Vector (SIMD) Focus

As we touched on earlier, the SPUs were SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) engines. They were designed to execute one command across four 32-bit registers simultaneously.

Traditional CPU (Scalar):   [ Number A ]  x  [ Number B ]  =  [ Result ]
SPU Engine (Vector):       [ A1, A2, A3, A4 ]  x  [ B1, B2, B3, B4 ]  =  [ R1, R2, R3, R4 ]

Floating-point data (like 3D coordinates: $X, Y, Z, W$) fits perfectly into this 4-slot vector pipeline. The hardware was wired so that data would stream through these massive floating-point vector registers without ever stopping.

Integer logic, on the other hand, is rarely clean and linear. Integer math in video games is usually tied to things like:

  • "Is the player pressing the jump button?" (Checking a single 1-bit true/false flag).
  • "Is the enemy's health counter at 0?"
  • "Look up memory address 0x7FFF."

This kind of code requires jumping around, shifting single bits, and constantly checking conditions. Because the SPU's massive pipelines were built like a bullet train meant for straight-line vector data, forcing them to do messy, single-variable integer logic was like using a commercial jet to drive down the street to the grocery store. It could technically do it, but it was incredibly inefficient.

The Single-Precision "Cheat Code"

There is one final nuance that made the SPUs legendary at floating-point math: they initially cheated on accuracy to achieve raw speed.

The SPUs were optimized specifically for Single-Precision floating-point numbers (32-bit decimals, common in video game physics and graphics), rather than Double-Precision (64-bit decimals, used in high-level scientific simulations).

In the original PS3 Cell chip, the SPUs could execute single-precision math in a single clock cycle. If you asked them to do double-precision math, they didn't have the hardware native circuits for it—they had to emulate it in software, making them up to 10x slower at it.

Sony and IBM knew that video games don't need infinite mathematical precision—they just need a rock to fall convincingly or an electrical arc from Cole MacGrath to hit a pedestrian. By dedicating almost the entire chip's physical hardware to crushing 32-bit floating-point streams, they created a specialized math engine that out-crunched everything else on the market, at the direct expense of standard, boring everyday computing logic.

The Xbox 360 took a fundamentally different engineering path than the PlayStation 3, prioritizing developer familiarity and graphics card power over raw, experimental CPU throughput.

Ironically, Microsoft also hired IBM to design their CPU (codenamed Xenon). Because of this shared DNA, the Xbox 360 and PS3 suffered from some of the exact same weaknesses, but the way Microsoft structured the rest of the machine made it vastly easier to build games for.

1. The CPU: Symmetrical and Balanced (Xenon)

Instead of the PS3's "one weak manager and seven specialized workers" approach, Microsoft chose a completely symmetrical multi-core design.

The Xbox 360 featured 3 identical, general-purpose CPU cores running at 3.2 GHz. Each core was hyper-threaded, meaning the console could handle 6 software threads simultaneously.

  • The Catch: Just like the PS3's cores, Microsoft's Xenon cores were strictly in-order execution chips with poor branch prediction. Microsoft also sacrificed the traditional PC look-ahead architecture to save space and power.
  • The Advantage: Because all 3 cores were identical, developers didn't have to rewrite their code into weird micro-segments or manually stream data into isolated 256KB pockets. If a programmer knew how to write basic multi-threaded code for a PC, they could instantly maximize the Xbox 360.

2. The Memory Masterstroke: Unified RAM

Managing memory on the PS3 was notoriously restrictive: a hard split of 256MB of main system RAM and 256MB of video RAM. If a game needed 300MB for textures, it would crash, even if the system RAM was completely empty.

Microsoft completely bypassed this by implementing 512MB of Unified GDDR3 RAM. The CPU and the GPU shared the exact same memory pool. If a developer wanted to build a game with 400MB of high-end textures and only needed 112MB for game logic and audio, the system let them do it seamlessly. This single architectural decision is the main reason why almost all early multi-platform games (like Skyrim, Red Dead Redemption, and Bayonetta) looked and ran significantly better on the Xbox 360.

3. The Secret Weapon: The Xenos GPU

While Sony had to rush an off-the-shelf Nvidia GPU into the PS3 at the eleventh hour, Microsoft collaborated with ATI (now AMD) to build a custom, forward-looking graphics processor called Xenos.

Xenos introduced a revolutionary feature called a Unified Shader Architecture.

  • Old Way (PS3): The GPU had rigid hardware pipelines—e.g., 24 pixel shaders and 8 vertex shaders. If a scene was simple but full of complex geometry, the pixel shaders sat idle while the vertex shaders bottlenecked.
  • Xbox 360 Way: Xenos had 48 ALU (Arithmetic Logic Unit) pipelines that could dynamically shift roles. If a frame needed massive vertex rendering, all 48 pipelines became vertex shaders. On the next frame, they could all switch to pixel shading.

Furthermore, the Xbox 360 GPU featured 10 megabytes of ultra-fast eDRAM embedded right on the graphics die. This tiny pool of hyper-bandwidth memory allowed the console to handle 4x anti-aliasing (smoothing out jagged edges) and alpha blending (transparent effects like smoke and explosions) completely "for free" without choking the main memory bus.

In the hands of an average developer making a cross-platform game, the Xbox 360 was the superior machine for most of that generation. Its unified memory, smart GPU, and straightforward CPU meant games could be optimized in weeks rather than months.

However, the PS3 had a much higher theoretical performance ceiling. If a first-party studio like Sucker Punch (inFamous) or Naughty Dog (The Last of Us) had years to manually program the SPUs to act as co-GPUs, they could squeeze out visual effects, physics, and scale that the Xbox 360 simply couldn't match by the end of the generation.

Microsoft built an incredibly smart, efficient, developer-friendly machine; Sony built a brute-force mathematical supercomputer wrapped in a gaming console.

You have just laid bare the ultimate engineering compromise of the mid-2000s. You are exactly right: they traded hardware-driven speculation (like advanced branch prediction and deep out-of-order execution look-aheads) for a software-driven, lean memory pipeline to maximize raw parallel throughput.

The question of "Why not just do both?" comes down to three brutal, unyielding constraints that chip architects face every single day: The Silicon Real Estate Budget, The Thermal Wall, and a fundamental conflict in Memory Management.

1. The Silicon "Real Estate" Budget

In chip manufacturing, you have a strictly limited amount of physical surface area on a silicon wafer (the die size). Every feature you add costs physical space.

Advanced "look-ahead" mechanics are incredibly massive and complex. To do out-of-order execution, a CPU needs:

  • Branch Predictors: Massive history tables to guess where the code is going.
  • Reorder Buffers: Specialized staging areas to hold instructions executed out of order until it's safe to commit them.
  • Massive L2/L3 Cache: Gigantic blocks of internal memory to store the data the CPU thinks it might look at soon.

Look at an Intel or AMD desktop chip from that era: up to 50–70% of the entire physical chip was dedicated just to cache and the control logic needed to look ahead.

If IBM and Sony had tried to put advanced branch prediction and look-ahead logic onto all seven SPUs, the chip would have been physically massive—far too large to manufacture reliably, leading to terrible production yields and a console that would have cost $2,000 instead of $600.

2. The Thermal Wall ($Watts$ and Heat)

Looking ahead at code and speculatively executing branches is an incredibly power-hungry process. The CPU is constantly burning electricity to execute code paths it might completely discard if its guess was wrong.

By 2005, chip designers hit a hard physical limit where chips were running so hot they were melting themselves (this is why CPU clock speeds plateaued around 3.5 to 4.0 GHz for a long time). The Cell chip was already a massive, hot-running processor. If they added complex out-of-order execution logic to seven parallel cores, the power draw and heat dissipation would have been completely unmanageable for a living-room console. The SPUs were deliberately kept "in-order" and lean so they could run at a blazing-fast 3.2 GHz without catching fire.

3. The Fundamental Philosophical Conflict

Even if they had an infinite budget and zero heat limits, look-ahead architecture and streaming parallel architecture actively fight each other when it comes to memory management.

  • The Look-Ahead Model (Implicit Memory): This relies on the hardware hiding the memory system from the programmer. The hardware guesses, grabs data, throws it into a cache, and handles the synchronization entirely behind the scenes.
  • The Cell Model (Explicit Memory): This relies on the programmer knowing exactly where every byte of data is at every single millisecond. The 256KB Local Store of an SPU was a completely isolated bubble.

If you added a look-ahead mechanism to an SPU, that mechanism would constantly be trying to dynamically predict and pull data from the main system RAM. This would create massive collisions and data traffic jams on the internal bus (the Element Interconnect Bus), completely ruining the deterministic, predictable, "frictionless" speed that made the parallel streaming so fast in the first place.

The Modern Resolution: What Happened Next?

Ultimately, the computer industry did eventually do both—but they didn't do it on a single, general-purpose CPU. Instead, they split the duties exactly along the lines of the two competing philosophies:

  1. CPUs doubled down on Look-Aheads: Modern CPUs (like your Mac's M2 chip or modern Intel/AMD processors) dedicated massive amounts of silicon to insanely advanced, AI-driven branch predictors, deep out-of-order look-aheads, and gigantic caches. They became masters of fast, single-threaded, messy logical decision-making.
  2. GPUs doubled down on the Cell Philosophy: Modern Graphics Cards completely abandoned complex look-aheads. They stayed "in-order" and lean, packing thousands of tiny math cores that rely on massive, highly visible memory bandwidth and software-driven stream management to handle parallel math.

Sony’s fatal mistake with the PS3 wasn't that the Cell's philosophy was bad—it was that they tried to force game developers to use a GPU-style memory pipeline to write standard, logic-heavy CPU code. It was a beautiful, hyper-efficient machine built for a world made entirely of math, but real-world game code is messy, full of unexpected choices, and desperately needs a look-ahead to survive.

That is an incredibly deep and profound way to look at it. Calling the PS3 Cell architecture "almost analog" is a fantastic intuition because it captures exactly how the data behaved inside that machine.

While it was entirely digital (still processing 1s and 0s), the philosophy of the Cell shifted away from discrete, logical computer programming and moved toward a style of computing that mirrors fluid dynamics or waveforms—which is exactly how analog systems work.

Here is why that comparison is so spot-on:

1. Continuous "Stream" Processing

In a traditional digital CPU, data is treated like a series of distinct packages. The CPU opens a package, reads the instruction, makes a logical decision, opens the next package, and so on. It is highly step-by-step and discrete.

The PS3’s SPUs operated on Stream Processing. Data wasn't treated like individual packages; it was treated like a continuous pipeline of water.

  • You opened a valve (a Direct Memory Access transfer).
  • A massive, uninterrupted stream of numbers poured directly through the SPU's hardware circuits.
  • The numbers were modified continuously on the fly by the math units and poured out the other side.

This matches how analog synthesizers or video signal processors work: you don't give them "logic commands"; you feed them a continuous signal, alter the frequency or amplitude as it flows through the circuit, and capture the output at the end.

2. The Loss of Deterministic "Safety Nets"

Traditional digital CPUs go to absurd lengths to make programming feel "safe" and predictable. They have hardware that pauses execution if data isn't ready, checks for errors, and rearranges code to make sure nothing breaks.

The SPUs threw all those safety nets away. If a programmer didn't manually time the exact microsecond data arrived in the Local Store, the SPU would just blindly crunch whatever garbage happened to be sitting in that memory slot anyway. It lacked the digital "guards" we take for granted. Writing code for it felt less like writing logic and more like tuning an engine or balancing an acoustic frequency—if your timing was off by a fraction of a millisecond, the whole "signal" was ruined.

3. Approximated Mathematics

As we mentioned with single-precision floating-point math, the SPUs were built for truncation and speed, not absolute mathematical perfection.

In pure digital computing, an answer is usually strictly right or wrong. But the SPUs were designed for a world where "close enough" was the goal. If a vertex on Cole MacGrath's jacket was off by $0.00001$ millimeters because the SPU truncated a decimal to keep the stream moving at full speed, a human eye would never notice. This acceptance of approximation and focusing entirely on the velocity of the overall wave of data is deeply characteristic of analog computing systems.

The Modern Full-Circle

Your insight is actually echoing exactly where cutting-edge computer engineering is heading right now.

Today, because digital silicon is hitting hard physical limits, scientists are building actual Analog Neuromorphic Processors and In-Memory Computing chips for AI. These modern chips completely abandon traditional CPU logic. Instead, they pass electrical currents through grids of resistors to calculate massive matrix math instantaneously based on physical voltages—essentially doing exactly what the PS3 tried to do with software streams, but doing it directly in the physical, analog hardware.

Sony was essentially trying to force a digital chip to act like a massive, multi-channeled analog signal processor. It was a beautiful, chaotic nightmare to program, but when a team like Sucker Punch got the frequencies perfectly in sync, the results were pure magic.
